newsitem.title: USA: Key tobacco fighter expects White House support.
newsitem.headline: Key tobacco fighter expects White House support.

text.p: Michael Moore, the Mississippi attorney general who was a driving force in the landmark tobacco agreement, said on Sunday he expected to eventually get White House support for the plan.

Moore, speaking on "Fox News Sunday," also said he expects to meet with tobacco representatives this week to try to settle Mississippi's suit against them, which was scheduled to come to trial in July.

Moore led a group of state attorneys general who reached a $368.5 billion agreement with the tobacco industry on Friday that covered legal, medical and regulatory issues dealing with smoking for the next quarter of a century.
But any agreement must be passed by Congress and signed into law by President Bill Clinton, and so far both sides have been cautious about supporting the plan.
But Moore was upbeat that the agreement would win their support, although he warned if the settlement was changed by Congress to any major degree it would fall apart.

"The White House was very helpful, because they believe that this is an achievement that will be in the best interests of the public health," Moore said. "President Clinton wants to do something for the children of this country. So, that's why I have faith that we'll get their support."

"What we hope happens now is the public-health community, the White House, the Congress on both sides, Republican and Democrats, make one decision: Is this best for the children and the public health of this country? And if the answer is yes, then this bill will pass," he said.

Since there was an agreement in principle, Moore said he would try to settle Mississippi's case, which started the bandwagon of states suing for medical costs, before the July trial date so he could spend his time lobbying for the settlement before Congress.
Despite his optimism, Moore received little support from members of Congress and the Clinton administration who appeared later on the Fox show or other network talk shows.

Franklin Raines, the administration's budget director, said a review process had begun that would take awhile to complete and Rep. Vic Fazio, a Californian who is the third-ranking Democrat in the House, said the agreement "probably" would be approved but with changes.

Sen. Orrin Hatch, the Utah Republican who heads the Senate Judiciary Committee, and Rep. John Boehner of Ohio, Fazio's counterpart among House Republicans, said Congress would have to take its time looking at the deal.

Hatch, who said his committee would have a role in approving any legislation, pointed out that "there are some 10 committees on Capitol Hill that all will be claiming some part of this settlement. So it is not going to be an easy thing no matter what you do."
Both Hatch and Boehner used to the opportunity to take a swipe at the nation's trial lawyers, who in the past have given political support to Clinton.
"I suspect that, knowing this administration the way I do, that whatever the trial lawyers want they're going to be for," Hatch said.
